title: Input Filtering — VIF and PCA on Correlated Aerodynamic Inputs
description: A wing aerodynamic dataset has 6 inputs: velocity, dynamic pressure, and Mach number are three ways to measure the same flight condition — highly correlated. Span and aspect ratio are geometrically related (aspect ratio scales with span in this dataset). You will use the Filter step to identify multicollinearity via VIF, then apply PCA to reduce 6 correlated inputs to 3 uncorrelated components before training. Read the 'Input Filtering & Dimensionality Reduction' topic in the Guide before starting.

steps.instruction: The dataset has 6 inputs: velocity (m/s), dynamic_q (Pa), mach (dimensionless), aoa (angle of attack, degrees), span (m), aspect_ratio. The output is cl (lift coefficient). Notice that velocity, dynamic_q, and mach all measure flight speed — they should be highly correlated.

quiz.question: If dynamic_q = 0.5 × ρ × velocity², what does that tell you about including both velocity and dynamic_q as model inputs?
options: Nothing — the model needs all available information
dynamic_q is derived directly from velocity, so they carry redundant information — including both inflates dimensionality without adding new signal
dynamic_q should replace velocity because it is more physical
They should be combined into a single input by averaging
quiz.explanation: When one input is a mathematical function of another (q = 0.5ρV²), they are by definition collinear. Their Pearson |r| will be near 1.0 and their VIF will be very large. Including both makes the model think there are two independent sources of information when there is really only one.

steps.instruction: Open the scatter matrix. Look at the velocity vs. dynamic_q and velocity vs. mach plots. You should see tight, nearly deterministic curves — confirming the physical relationship between these variables.

quiz.question: In the scatter matrix, a curved but tight relationship between two inputs suggests:
options: A linear correlation that GPR will handle automatically
A nonlinear but nearly deterministic relationship — the two inputs are functionally dependent and one is redundant
The data needs to be cleaned before correlations can be assessed
These inputs will cause the surrogate to overfit
quiz.explanation: Pearson r only measures linear correlation. Two variables can have |r| < 1 but still be nearly perfectly redundant if their relationship is nonlinear (e.g. q ∝ V²). The VIF table in the Filter step catches both linear and nonlinear multicollinearity because it measures how well each input is predicted by all the others.

steps.instruction: Assign all six inputs (velocity, dynamic_q, mach, aoa, span, aspect_ratio) as Input and cl as Output.

Apply Min-Max normalization to all 6 inputs. Normalization is especially important before PCA — PCA uses variance, and variables with large ranges would otherwise dominate the principal components regardless of their physical importance.

quiz.question: Why must inputs be normalized before PCA?
options: PCA requires inputs to sum to 1.0

PCA finds directions of maximum variance; without normalization, inputs with large numeric ranges (e.g. dynamic_q in Pa vs. mach ≈ 0.3) dominate the components purely due to scale, not physical importance
Normalization is only needed for GPR, not PCA
PCA automatically normalizes internally so this step does not matter
quiz.explanation: dynamic_q ranges up to ~24,000 Pa while mach ranges ~0.15–0.58. Without normalization, PCA's first component would be almost entirely dynamic_q — not because it carries the most information, but because it has the largest numeric spread. Min-Max scaling puts all inputs on [0, 1] so PCA responds to information content, not measurement units.

steps.instruction: Open Step 7 — Filter. Click 'Analyze →'. Look at the VIF table. You should see: velocity and mach with VIF > 1000 (nearly perfectly collinear — mach = velocity / speed_of_sound); dynamic_q with VIF ~40 (high, but lower because the V² relationship is nonlinear, so linear VIF underestimates it); span and aspect_ratio with VIF ~20 (aspect_ratio ≈ 2.5 × span in this dataset); aoa near 1 (independent).

quiz.question: VIF = 40 for dynamic_q means:
options: dynamic_q explains 40% of the output variance
dynamic_q can be predicted from the other inputs with R² ≈ 0.975 — it carries very little independent information
The model trained with dynamic_q will have 40× more error
You should always remove inputs with VIF > 10
quiz.explanation: VIF = 1/(1 − R²), where R² measures how well that input is predicted by all other inputs — not by the output. VIF = 40 means R² ≈ 1 − 1/40 = 0.975: 97.5% of dynamic_q's variance is already explained by the other inputs (mainly velocity and mach). It contributes almost nothing new. Note: the decision to remove or use PCA is yours — the tool flags, you decide.

steps.instruction: Scroll to the bottom of the Filter panel and open the 'PCA Dimensionality Reduction' section. Set Components to 3 and click 'Preview PCA →'. Look at the explained-variance chart. PC1 and PC2 should capture the two correlated groups (speed and geometry). PC3 adds aoa's contribution.

quiz.question: The PCA preview shows that 3 components explain >99% of variance. The suggested auto-threshold (≥90%) is also 3. What does this tell you?
options: 3 inputs contain all the information; the other 3 can be dropped safely
There are exactly 3 independent sources of variation in the 6 inputs — the three correlated groups each collapse into one component
The model will train 3× faster with 3 components
You must use exactly 3 components or the model will be wrong
quiz.explanation: PCA reveals the intrinsic dimensionality of the input space. 6 inputs with 3 internal correlation groups contain only ~3 independent sources of information. PC1 captures the flight-speed cluster (velocity, dynamic_q, mach all vary together). PC2 captures the geometry cluster (span, aspect_ratio). PC3 captures aoa, which is independent of both groups. >99% retained means the original 6 inputs genuinely reduce to 3 degrees of freedom.

steps.instruction: Click 'Apply PCA →' to replace the 6 correlated inputs with 3 principal components. A success message will confirm. Note: the model and prediction steps will now use PC coordinates (PC1, PC2, PC3) — not the original physical variables.
Open Step 8 — Model. Configure a GPR with test split 0.2, 5-fold CV. Train. With only 3 uncorrelated inputs, GPR should fit efficiently.

Review the R² score and parity plot. A well-tuned PCA + GPR pipeline on this dataset should achieve R² > 0.90. If R² is lower, the discarded variance may include some aoa signal — try 4 components and retrain.

quiz.question: The PCA + GPR pipeline achieves higher R² than a GPR trained on all 6 original inputs without filtering. What is the most likely explanation?
options: PCA always improves R² — it is a free performance boost
Removing collinear inputs stabilised the GPR kernel optimisation. Multicollinearity causes the kernel to see multiple inputs as equivalent, degrading length-scale estimates and model accuracy
The test set happened to be easier after PCA
Fewer inputs always outperform more inputs in GPR
quiz.explanation: GPR uses a kernel (e.g. RBF) to compute distances between points in input space. When three inputs all measure the same thing (velocity, q, Mach), the kernel treats flight speed as three dimensions instead of one, distorting the distance metric. PCA collapses the three correlated inputs into one component, giving the kernel an accurate view of the actual degrees of freedom.

steps.instruction: Open Step 10 — Predict. Notice that the input fields show the original physical variables (velocity, dynamic_q, mach, aoa, span, aspect_ratio) — not PC coordinates. A 'PCA active' banner confirms the transform is handled automatically: the toolkit normalizes your values, applies the stored 3-component PCA matrix, and passes the resulting PC coordinates to the GPR. The fields pre-fill with the training means — click 'Run Prediction' to observe the predicted cl.

quiz.question: The PCA + GPR pipeline accepts physical inputs and predicts correctly. What interpretability trade-off remains?
options: You can no longer predict at arbitrary velocity values — only near the training means

The GPR kernel operates in PC space, so its length-scales describe sensitivity to PC1/PC2/PC3, not directly to velocity or aoa. You cannot read off which physical variable most influences the output without examining PCA loadings or running a sensitivity analysis
Predicted cl values will always be less accurate than a GPR trained directly on the 6 physical inputs
Batch prediction is disabled after PCA is applied
quiz.explanation: Prediction at any physical operating point works correctly — the toolkit applies normalization and the stored PCA transform automatically. The remaining trade-off is interpretability: the GPR's internal length-scales correspond to PC components, not physical variables. To understand whether velocity or aoa is the dominant driver, you would examine the PCA loading matrix (which physical variables load heavily on each PC) or run a one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis in the Sensitivity step.
